newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan output rises, but outlook still uncertain.
newsitem.headline: Japan output rises, but outlook still uncertain.

text.p: Japan's industrial output showed a strong rise in January, according to figures released on Thursday, but economists said uncertainties still loom ahead of a planned tax hike from April.

Industrial production in January rose a preliminary 5.3 percent from December, up sharply from a modest 0.1 percent rise in December and a bit higher than an economists' poll which had shown an average forecast of a 4.9 percent rise.
Currency dealers said the slightly higher-than-expected rise, along with firmer money rates, led to purchases of yen against the dollar in the Tokyo foreign exchange market.
"The market saw the rise in the output as showing that the state of the economy is not so bad after all," said Koji Asano, senior manager of foreign exchange department at Fuji Bank.
In late Thursday Tokyo trade, the yen was standing at around 120.50 to the dollar, up from 122.20 in New York on Wednesday.
But the stock market failed to react to the output data, and the benchmark Nikkei average closed nearly flat at 19,021.56 up just 0.16 percent.
Economists said the January rise was temporary, affected largely by buying ahead of a planned April 1 rise in the national sales tax from three percent to five percent.

"We are seeing a lot of the pre-consumption tax demand coming through... so that I would expect that production would be scaled back in the next couple of months from this quite large increase," said Peter Morgan, senior economist with HSBC James Capel Japan.
The Trade Ministry also forecast that manufacturers' output will decrease 3.3 percent month-on-month in February and fall 2.7 percent in March.

"The (forecasted fall) for February and March will cancel out any increase in January. So production will be quite flat in the coming two months," said Mikihiro Matsuoka, senior economist at Daiwa Institute of Research.
Economists also said the weak output expected in the next two months reflects the uncertainty held by firms over the economic outlook beyond April.

"Businesses cannot maintain a clear outlook on the economy as they want to see the effects of the fiscal tightening measures to be taken from April." said Kyohei Morita, economist at Nomura Research Institute.
